claim: PTPRK is stabilized at cell-cell contacts in epithelial cells.
source: We report here that the homophilic receptor PTPRK is stabilized at cell-cell contacts in epithelial cells.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data showing PTPRK localization at cell-cell contacts (Figure 1B) and co-culture experiments (Figure 1C).

claim: PTPRK directly and selectively dephosphorylates at least five substrates, including Afadin, PARD3 and δ-catenin family members.
source: PTPRK directly and selectively dephosphorylates at least five substrates, including Afadin, PARD3 and δ-catenin family members, which are all important cell-cell adhesion regulators.
evidence: Supported by dephosphorylation assays (Figure 5), phosphoproteomics data (Figure 3), and interaction studies (Figure 2).

claim: Loss of PTPRK phosphatase activity leads to disrupted cell junctions and increased invasive characteristics.
source: In line with this, loss of PTPRK phosphatase activity leads to disrupted cell junctions and increased invasive characteristics.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy showing disrupted junctions (Figure 7A), TEER measurements (Figure 7C), and spheroid invasion assays (Figure 8).

claim: PTPRK forms homophilic interactions in trans at cell-cell contacts.
source: To investigate homophilic PTPRK interactions in cells, we generated CRISPR/Cas9 PTPRK knockout (KO) MCF10A cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), stably expressing nuclear mApple, and co-cultured them with unlabeled wildtype cells. By immunostaining, PTPRK is strikingly absent from cell-cell contacts between wildtype and adjacent KO cells, despite expression of other R2B receptors (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by co-culture experiments showing PTPRK absence at wildtype-KO cell contacts (Figure 1C).

claim: PTPRK protein levels increase with increasing cell density.
source: Consistently, PTPRK protein levels increase with increasing cell density (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis at different cell densities (Figure 1D).

claim: Screening recombinant PTPRK ECD against a secreted protein microarray did not identify any additional ligands.
source: Finally, screening recombinant PTPRK ECD against a secreted protein microarray did not identify any additional ligands (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by protein microarray screening data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).

claim: Homophilic trans-interactions stabilize PTPRK at cell-cell contacts in epithelial cells.
source: Thus, in combination, our data indicates homophilic trans-interactions stabilize PTPRK at cell-cell contacts in epithelial cells.
evidence: Inferred from co-culture experiments, density-dependent expression, and microarray screening results.

claim: PTPRK localizes to puncta at basal cell-cell contacts that partially overlap with E-Cadherin in MCF10A epithelial cells.
source: Using one of our antibodies for structured illumination microscopy, we found PTPRK localized to puncta at basal cell-cell contacts that partially overlap with the adherens junction (AJ) protein E-Cadherin in MCF10A epithelial cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by structured illumination microscopy images (Figure 1B).

claim: The R2B receptor family form homophilic interactions and have been proposed to respond to cell-cell contact.
source: The R2B RPTP subfamily form homophilic interactions and have been proposed to respond to cell-cell contact (Aricescu et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: There are four human R2B receptors: PTPRK, PTPRM, PTPRT and PTPRU.
source: There are four human R2B receptors: PTPRK, PTPRM, PTPRT and PTPRU, which share a common domain architecture of one MAM (meprin/A5/μ), one immunoglobulin (Ig)-like and four fibronectin (FN) domains combined with an uncharacterized juxtamembrane domain and tandem intracellular phosphatase domains; the first active (D1) and the second inactive (D2) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of R2B receptor family structure.

claim: PTPRK was identified as a candidate driver gene in mouse intestinal tumorigenesis by insertional mutagenesis.
source: Its paralog PTPRK was identified as a candidate driver gene in mouse intestinal tumorigenesis by insertional mutagenesis (March et al., 2011; Starr et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PTPRK was identified as a gene fusion partner with the oncogene RSPO3 in a subset of human colorectal cancers.
source: and was more recently identified as a gene fusion partner with the oncogene RSPO3 in a subset of human colorectal cancers (Seshagiri et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within the PTPRK genic region are associated with inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs) and type I diabetes age of onset.
source: Furthermore, single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within the PTPRK genic region are associated with inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs) and type I diabetes age of onset (Inshaw et al., 2018; Trynka et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PTPRK is regulated by a proteolytic cascade involving furin, ADAM10 and γ-secretase.
source: PTPRK is regulated by a proteolytic cascade involving furin, ADAM10 and γ-secretase (Anders et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: PTPRK might function to dephosphorylate proteins such as EGFR or STAT3.
source: and might function to dephosphorylate proteins such as EGFR (Xu et al., 2005) or STAT3 (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies, but presented as speculative ('might').

claim: PTPRK mRNA is broadly expressed, except in immune cells, skeletal muscle and testes.
source: PTPRK mRNA is broadly expressed, except in immune cells, skeletal muscle and testes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by mRNA expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PTPRK is upregulated by transforming growth factor β (TGFβ) signaling.
source: and is upregulated by transforming growth factor β (TGFβ) signaling (Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Sixty-four proteins were >2 fold enriched (p<0.05; n = 4) on the wildtype PTPRK-ICD.
source: Sixty-four proteins were >2 fold enriched (p<0.05; n = 4) on the wildtype PTPRK-ICD (Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data from pull-down experiments.

claim: Only 21% of the PTPRK-ICD interactome overlapped between MCF10A and Hs27 cells.
source: We found that only 21% of the PTPRK-ICD interactome overlapped between MCF10A and Hs27 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), which might reflect differences in protein expression or phosphorylation between the cell lines.
evidence: Supported by comparison of mass spectrometry data from two cell lines.

claim: The first substrate trap (D1057A) enriched the serine/threonine kinase MAP4K4 and RAPGEF6.
source: The first substrate trap (D1057A) enriched the serine/threonine kinase MAP4K4 and RAPGEF6, which were both recently linked to Hippo signaling (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; Meng et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data from substrate-trapping experiments.

claim: FMRP and the cell junction associated proteins PARD3, Afadin (AF-6/MLLT4) and PLEKHA6 were enriched on the second substrate trap (C1089S).
source: FMRP and the cell junction associated proteins PARD3, Afadin (AF-6/MLLT4) and PLEKHA6 were enriched on the second substrate trap (C1089S; Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data from substrate-trapping experiments.

claim: Gene ontology (GO) term analysis for the PTPRK interactome highlights the enrichment of cell junction proteins across all domains.
source: Gene ontology (GO) term analysis for the PTPRK interactome highlights the enrichment of cell junction proteins across all domains (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis of mass spectrometry data.

claim: The MAP4K4 interaction with PTPRK D1057A ICD from pervanadate lysates was competed using orthovanadate, consistent with phosphotyrosine-mediated trapping.
source: The MAP4K4 interaction with PTPRK D1057A ICD from pervanadate lysates was competed using orthovanadate, consistent with phosphotyrosine-mediated trapping (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by vanadate competition experiments shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Afadin was not depleted by orthovanadate treatment.
source: In contrast, Afadin was not depleted by orthovanadate treatment.
evidence: Supported by vanadate competition experiments shown in Figure 2H.

claim: PARD3, PKP4 and p120Cat bind the C1089S ICD less effectively in the absence of phosphorylation.
source: Furthermore, PARD3, PKP4 and p120Cat bind the C1089S ICD less effectively in the absence of phosphorylation, also supporting the efficacy of the trapping approach (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by dephosphorylation experiments shown in Figure 2I.

claim: All substrate-trapped proteins could still interact with PTPRK domains in phosphatase-treated lysates.
source: However, we noted that all substrate-trapped proteins could still interact with PTPRK domains in phosphatase-treated lysates (Figure 2H and I)
evidence: Supported by experiments with dephosphorylated lysates.

claim: Most interactors can bind to the enzymatically active WT ICD.
source: and most interactors can bind to the enzymatically active WT ICD (Figure 2F and G), indicating phosphorylation-independent PTPRK interactions.
evidence: Supported by pull-down experiments with wildtype PTPRK-ICD.

claim: The PTPRK-D2 domain alone was sufficient to pull down approximately a third of PTPRK ICD interactors.
source: Furthermore, the PTPRK-D2 domain alone was sufficient to pull down approximately a third of PTPRK ICD interactors (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B; Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by pull-down experiments with PTPRK-D2 domain.

claim: Many proteins can bind PTPRK independently of phosphorylation or to its D2 pseudophosphatase domain.
source: Although substrate trapping was effective, our data indicate that because many proteins can bind PTPRK independently of phosphorylation or to its D2 pseudophosphatase domain (Figure 2F and G), trapping approaches alone could miss potential substrates.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations including vanadate competition and D2 domain pull-downs.

claim: Afadin, RAPGEF6 and NUFIP2 interact specifically with PTPRK.
source: Afadin, RAPGEF6 and NUFIP2 interact specifically with PTPRK, indicated by their biased depletion from supernatants.
evidence: Supported by comparative pull-down experiments with PTPRK and PTPRM ICDs.

claim: PARD3 and PKP4 bind both PTPRK and PTPRM ICDs.
source: Interestingly, we found several that bound both PTPRK and PTPRM ICDs such as PARD3 and PKP4.
evidence: Supported by pull-down experiments with both PTPRK and PTPRM ICDs.

claim: MAP4K4, MINK1, PTPN14, DLG5 and p120Cat have a higher affinity for PTPRK than PTPRM in pull downs.
source: Although MAP4K4, MINK1, PTPN14, DLG5 and p120Cat are depleted by both ICDs, they appear to have a higher affinity for PTPRK in pull downs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D and E).
evidence: Supported by comparative pull-down experiments.

claim: PTPRK and PTPRM have both unique and redundant roles at cell junctions.
source: Overall, the PTPRK interactome is enriched with cell junction-related proteins and shows partial overlap with PTPRM. Together, these data suggest that PTPRK and PTPRM have both unique and redundant roles at cell junctions.
evidence: Inferred from comparative analysis of PTPRK and PTPRM interactomes.

claim: 282 quantifiable phosphotyrosine sites on 185 proteins were identified from three experiments.
source: We identified 282 quantifiable phosphotyrosine sites on 185 proteins (Figure 3—source data 1) from three experiments.
evidence: Supported by quantitative phosphoproteomics data.

claim: 15 phosphosites were statistically upregulated in PTPRK KO cells compared to wildtype in at least two experiments.
source: Interestingly, 15 phosphosites were statistically upregulated in PTPRK KO cells compared to wildtype in at least two experiments, but only one site, in PAG1, was down regulated (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative phosphoproteomics data.

claim: Afadin, PARD3 and PLEKHA6 were amongst the proteins possessing enriched phosphosites in PTPRK KO cells.
source: Strikingly, Afadin, PARD3 and PLEKHA6, which were all 'substrate-trapped' by PTPRK-C1089S, were amongst the proteins possessing enriched phosphosites in PTPRK KO cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative phosphoproteomics data showing hyperphosphorylation in PTPRK KO cells.

claim: Upregulated phosphorylation was identified in at least one experiment for p120Cat, PKP2, PKP3 and PKP4.
source: Moreover, we identified upregulated phosphorylation in at least one experiment for p120Cat, PKP2, PKP3 and PKP4, which are δ-catenin family proteins and interact with the PTPRK ICD (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative phosphoproteomics data.

claim: The observed phosphosite levels on all proteins were not due to differences in protein amounts, except for PLEKHA6.
source: Critically, our total proteome analysis showed that the observed phosphosite levels on all proteins were not due to differences in protein amounts, except for PLEKHA6, which was not quantified (Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by total proteome analysis.

claim: PTPRK KO cells showed downregulation of epithelial markers such as Keratin14, and upregulation of several mesenchymal markers such as vitronectin (VTN).
source: Our analysis of PTPRK KO cells showed downregulation of epithelial markers such as Keratin14, and upregulation of several mesenchymal markers such as vitronectin (VTN; Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by total proteome analysis.

claim: By combining the PTPRK interactome with tyrosine phosphoproteomics, eight candidate substrates were identified.
source: Thus, by combining the PTPRK interactome with tyrosine phosphoproteomics we have identified eight candidate substrates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inferred from integration of interactome and phosphoproteomics data.

claim: PTPRK showed reduced activity against peptides with basic residues in the three positions N-terminal to phosphotyrosine.
source: Previously, Barr et al. (2009) tested recombinant PTPs against a panel of phosphopeptides and observed limited sequence selectivity. For example, PTPRK showed reduced activity against peptides with basic residues in the three positions N-terminal to phosphotyrosine, including an EGFR-pY1068-containing peptide.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: PTPRB showed no sequence preference.
source: In contrast, PTPRB showed no sequence preference (Barr et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The consensus sequence showed a slight bias against basic residues immediately adjacent to the phosphotyrosine.
source: To investigate whether our candidate substrates shared common features we generated a consensus sequence, which showed a slight bias against basic residues immediately adjacent to the phosphotyrosine (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis of candidate substrates.

claim: The positively charged PTPRK active site entrance may preclude binding of positively charged or basic amino acids.
source: This is consistent with the positively charged PTPRK active site entrance observed in its crystal structure, which may preclude binding of positively charged or basic amino acids (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Inferred from structural analysis of PTPRK.

claim: Several phosphosites identified are growth factor- and, in most cases, Src kinase-dependent.
source: Interestingly, several phosphosites identified here are growth factor- and, in most cases, Src kinase-dependent (Reddy et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The Src family kinase activating phosphotyrosine (e.g. Src-Y419) is 1.6-fold lower in PTPRK KO cells.
source: Importantly, however, the Src family kinase activating phosphotyrosine (e.g. Src-Y419) is 1.6-fold lower in PTPRK KO cells, therefore such kinase activity does not explain the observed differences (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by phosphoproteomics data.

claim: PTPRK influences the tyrosine phosphorylation of numerous interacting proteins in cells, suggesting it has non-redundant cellular phosphatase activity.
source: Thus, PTPRK influences the tyrosine phosphorylation of numerous interacting proteins in cells, suggesting it has non-redundant cellular phosphatase activity.
evidence: Inferred from phosphoproteomics data showing multiple hyperphosphorylated proteins in PTPRK KO cells.

claim: Truncated PTPRK showed notably stronger staining at the cell surface than PTPRK-C1089S.
source: Truncated PTPRK showed notably stronger staining at the cell surface than PTPRK-C1089S, perhaps reflecting the loss of an endocytic or degradative signal in the ICD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data and speculative interpretation.

claim: Afadin, PARD3, p120Cat, PKP3, PKP4, ABLIM3 and EGFR were enriched on PTPRK-C1089S over the truncated form.
source: Immunoblots of pulldowns from doxycycline-induced, confluent cells revealed enrichment on PTPRK-C1089S over the truncated form for the candidate substrates Afadin, PARD3, p120Cat, PKP3, PKP4, as well as ABLIM3 and EGFR, but not E-Cadherin, Paxillin, β-Catenin, Tubulin or ZO2 (Figure 4A and B, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by BioID experiments.

claim: MINK1, PKP4, PTPN14 and DLG5 were enriched and were previously identified by PTPRK BioID in HEK293 cells.
source: Importantly, MINK1, PKP4, PTPN14 and DLG5 were also enriched and were previously identified by PTPRK BioID in HEK293 cells (St-Denis et al., 2016), lending additional support to our observations (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by BioID experiments and citation to previous study.

claim: A three-fold higher molar ratio of PTPRM was required to match PTPRK activity.
source: Using an in vitro para-nitrophenylphosphate (pNPP) colorimetric dephosphorylation assay, we determined that a three-fold higher molar ratio of PTPRM was required to match PTPRK activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), consistent with a previous study (Barr et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by pNPP assay data and citation to previous study.

claim: A three-fold higher molar ratio of PTPRK-ICD was required for equivalent activity to the D1 domain, suggesting the D2 reduces D1 enzyme activity.
source: Interestingly, a three-fold higher molar ratio of PTPRK-ICD was required for equivalent activity to the D1 domain, suggesting the D2 reduces D1 enzyme activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by pNPP assay data and inference about D2 domain function.

claim: E-Cadherin, STAT3, β-Catenin, Paxillin and EGFR-pY1068 were not dephosphorylated by either PTPRK or PTPRM under these conditions.
source: Consistent with our interaction data, several previously reported R2B receptor substrates including E-Cadherin, STAT3, β-Catenin, Paxillin and EGFR-pY1068 (Duan et al., 2015), were not dephosphorylated by either PTPRK or PTPRM under these conditions (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: Supported by in-lysate dephosphorylation assays.

claim: The PTPRK ICD, but not the PTPRK-D1 or PTPRM domains, completely dephosphorylated Afadin.
source: In contrast, the PTPRK ICD, but strikingly not the PTPRK-D1 or PTPRM domains, completely dephosphorylated Afadin (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a combined role for the D1 and D2 domains in its recognition and selective dephosphorylation.
evidence: Supported by in-lysate dephosphorylation assays.

claim: PARD3 and PKP3 were preferentially dephosphorylated by the PTPRK and PTPRM ICDs.
source: PARD3 and PKP3 were preferentially dephosphorylated by the PTPRK and PTPRM ICDs.
evidence: Supported by in-lysate dephosphorylation assays.

claim: The PTPRK and PTPRM D1 domains alone were sufficient to dephosphorylate ABLIM3, PKP4 and p120Cat.
source: In contrast, the PTPRK and PTPRM D1 domains alone were sufficient to dephosphorylate ABLIM3, PKP4 and p120Cat (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by in-lysate dephosphorylation assays.

claim: Addition of PTPRK-D2 to PTPRK-D1 did not affect its activity against p120Cat.
source: However, addition of PTPRK-D2 to PTPRK-D1 did not affect its activity against, for example, p120Cat (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by in-lysate dephosphorylation assays.

claim: PTPRM and PTPRK have overlapping substrate specificities for δ-catenin proteins, ABLIM3 and PARD3.
source: In combination with our interaction studies, these data suggest that PTPRM and PTPRK have overlapping substrate specificities for δ-catenin proteins, ABLIM3 and PARD3, and the PTPRK-ICD selectively dephosphorylates Afadin.
evidence: Inferred from dephosphorylation assays and interaction studies.

claim: The PTPRK-D2 domain is sufficient to recruit Afadin for dephosphorylation by PTPRM-D1.
source: Strikingly, the PTPRK-D2 domain is sufficient to recruit Afadin for dephosphorylation by PTPRM-D1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by dephosphorylation assays with chimeric proteins.

claim: p120Cat is dephosphorylated by all domains, based on its presence in the associated supernatants.
source: In contrast, p120Cat is dephosphorylated by all domains, based on its presence in the associated supernatants (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by dephosphorylation assays with chimeric proteins.

claim: Paxillin is not dephosphorylated by any PTPRK or PTPRM combinations.
source: Consistent with our previous findings, Paxillin is not dephosphorylated by any PTPRK or PTPRM combinations (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by dephosphorylation assays with chimeric proteins.

claim: PTPRK and PTPRM can directly and selectively dephosphorylate substrates.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that PTPRK and PTPRM can directly and selectively dephosphorylate substrates, and that the D2 pseudophosphatase domain is necessary and sufficient for recruitment of the PTPRK-specific substrate, Afadin.
evidence: Inferred from multiple dephosphorylation assays.

claim: The D2 pseudophosphatase domain is necessary and sufficient for recruitment of the PTPRK-specific substrate, Afadin.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that PTPRK and PTPRM can directly and selectively dephosphorylate substrates, and that the D2 pseudophosphatase domain is necessary and sufficient for recruitment of the PTPRK-specific substrate, Afadin.
evidence: Inferred from dephosphorylation assays with chimeric proteins.

claim: Afadin binding to the PTPRK D2 domain is not mediated by phosphotyrosine.
source: We were unable to deplete Afadin from the PTPRK D2 domain with vanadate or dephosphorylation of cell lysates, suggesting binding is not mediated by phosphotyrosine (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by vanadate competition and dephosphorylation experiments.

claim: Mutations to reactivate the PTPRK D2 domain had no impact on D2 domain activity.
source: Using a pNPP assay, we found no impact of the mutations on D2 domain activity (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), similar to recent failed attempts to reactivate the PTPRE D2 domain (Lountos et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by pNPP assay data and citation to previous study.

claim: The D2 domain mutations did not abrogate binding to several interactors.
source: Importantly, the D2 domain mutations did not abrogate binding to several interactors (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by pull-down experiments with mutant D2 domain.

claim: The surface charge surrounding the putative active site of PTPRK D2 domain significantly diverges from that of the D1 domain.
source: We generated a homology model for the PTPRK D2 domain based on PTPRE, and found that the surface charge surrounding the putative active site significantly diverges from that of the D1 domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: Supported by homology modeling.

claim: The D2 domain substrate recognition mechanism does not require substrate phosphorylation.
source: These data suggest the D2 domain substrate recognition mechanism does not require substrate phosphorylation, which is consistent with our earlier findings (Figure 2H and I) as well as PTPRK D2 domain structural and sequence features.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations and structural analysis.

claim: PTPRK-D1 and ICD, but not the catalytically inactive PTPRK-C1089S, almost completely dephosphorylated both p120Cat-pY228 and -pY904 sites.
source: In contrast, PTPRK-D1 and ICD, but not the catalytically inactive PTPRK-C1089S (Figure 6A) or pervanadate-inhibited PTPRK ICD (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), almost completely dephosphorylated both p120Cat-pY228 and -pY904 sites.
evidence: Supported by in-lysate dephosphorylation assays with site-specific antibodies.

claim: PTPRM also dephosphorylated both p120Cat-pY228 and -pY904 sites.
source: PTPRM also dephosphorylated both sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by in-lysate dephosphorylation assays.

claim: p120Cat-pY257 levels were unchanged in PTPRK KO cells by phosphoproteomics.
source: Combined with the observation that p120Cat-pY257 levels were unchanged in PTPRK KO cells by phosphoproteomics (Figure 3—source data 1) our data are consistent with PTPRK site selectivity, at least for p120Cat.
evidence: Supported by phosphoproteomics data.

claim: p120Cat-pY228 and -pY904 are increased on average 3–4-fold in confluent PTPRK KO cells compared to wildtype.
source: Immunoblotting confirms that p120Cat-pY228 and -pY904 are increased on average 3–4-fold in confluent PTPRK KO cells compared to wildtype, whereas Paxillin-pY118 is unchanged, consistent with our phosphoproteomics results (n = 4; Figure 6B and C; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis.

claim: Doxycycline-induction of PTPRK, but not the C1089S mutant, in PTPRK KO cells reproducibly and dose-dependently reduced p120Cat-pY228 and -pY904 levels.
source: Doxycycline-induction of PTPRK, but not the C1089S mutant, in PTPRK KO cells reproducibly and dose-dependently reduced p120Cat-pY228 and -pY904 levels, without affecting total p120Cat (n = 5; Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments with inducible PTPRK expression.

claim: Reintroduction of PTPRK did not affect Paxillin-pY118.
source: Conversely, reintroduction of PTPRK did not affect Paxillin-pY118.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments.

claim: PTPRK is an active and selective tyrosine phosphatase for p120Cat in confluent MCF10A cells.
source: These results suggest PTPRK is an active and selective tyrosine phosphatase for p120Cat in confluent MCF10A cells.
evidence: Inferred from dephosphorylation assays and rescue experiments.

claim: Afadin, PARD3, PKP3, PKP4, and p120Cat are high confidence substrates for PTPRK.
source: We have demonstrated that Afadin, PARD3, PKP3, PKP4, and p120Cat are high confidence substrates for PTPRK, with PLEKHA6, MAP4K4, PKP2, KIAA1217, ABLIM3 and Girdin also being good candidates.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including interaction studies, phosphoproteomics, and dephosphorylation assays.

claim: Wildtype cells were more closely packed and organized than PTPRK KO cells, which exhibited large gaps between cells.
source: Wildtype cells were more closely packed and organized than PTPRK KO cells, which exhibited large gaps between cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images.

claim: A striking reduction in cell height was observed in PTPRK KO cells.
source: Moreover, we observed a striking reduction in cell height in PTPRK KO cells (Figure 7A (inset) and 7B).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy measurements.

claim: PTPRK KO cells exhibited a ~ 50% reduction in TEER and a small but significant increase in FITC-dextran permeability compared to wildtype cells.
source: PTPRK KO cells exhibited a ~ 50% reduction in TEER and a small but significant increase in FITC-dextran permeability compared to wildtype cells indicating a leakier monolayer (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by TEER measurements and permeability assays.

claim: TEER measurements were partially rescued by reintroduction of PTPRK, but not a catalytically inactive mutant.
source: TEER measurements were partially rescued by reintroduction of PTPRK, but not a catalytically inactive mutant (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by TEER measurements in rescue experiments.

claim: PTPRK KO cells displayed a ~ 20% decrease in the intensity of F-actin, E-Cadherin, Desmoglein 3 (DSG3) and p120Cat.
source: Consistent with this altered organization, immunostained PTPRK KO cells grown on coverslips displayed a ~ 20% decrease in the intensity of F-actin, the AJ protein E-Cadherin, the desmosomal protein Desmoglein 3 (DSG3) and the PTPRK substrate p120Cat (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification.

claim: The junctional markers displayed reduced colocalization with F-actin in PTPRK KO cells.
source: The junctional markers also displayed reduced colocalization with F-actin (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis of immunofluorescence images.

claim: The levels of junctional proteins were unaffected by PTPRK loss.
source: However, the levels of these junctional proteins were unaffected by PTPRK loss (Figure 6B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis.

claim: Reintroduction of PTPRK or PTPRK-C1089S was able to partially rescue E-Cadherin intensity.
source: Reintroduction of PTPRK or PTPRK-C1089S was able to partially rescue E-Cadherin intensity (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification in rescue experiments.

claim: Catalytic activity was required to rescue F-actin intensity.
source: however, catalytic activity was required to rescue F-actin intensity (Figure 7D–E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence quantification in rescue experiments.

claim: Rescue of E-Cadherin and F-actin colocalization requires PTPRK D1 domain activity.
source: In line with this, rescue of E-Cadherin and F-actin colocalization requires PTPRK D1 domain activity, suggesting PTPRK substrate hyperphosphorylation contributes to impaired junctional integrity.
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis in rescue experiments and inference about mechanism.

claim: shRNAs targeting PTPRK in MCF10A cells perturbs their morphogenesis in 3D culture.
source: It has previously been reported that shRNAs targeting PTPRK in MCF10A cells perturbs their morphogenesis in 3D culture (Ramesh et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: PTPRK KO cells mostly form normal acini.
source: We find PTPRK KO cells mostly form normal acini (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by 3D culture experiments.

claim: ~20% of PTPRK KO spheroids exhibited a branched or protrusive morphology after 14 days in culture.
source: however,~20% exhibited a branched or protrusive morphology after 14 days in culture (Figure 8B), resembling the previously described invasive behavior observed upon combined EGFR and Src overexpression in MCF10A cells (Dimri et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by quantification of spheroid morphology and citation to previous study.

claim: PTPRK KO spheroids showed normal apical polarization of the Golgi.
source: When we collected intact spheroids for immunostaining we found normal apical polarization of the Golgi (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining of spheroids.

claim: PTPRK KO spheroids were significantly larger, by diameter, than wildtype.
source: However, PTPRK KO spheroids were significantly larger, by diameter, than wildtype (Figure 8D), despite similar proliferation rates of subconfluent cells in 2D (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by spheroid diameter measurements and proliferation assays.

claim: PTPRK functions in promoting cell-cell junctions and repressing invasive behavior, probably through recruitment and dephosphorylation of several cell junction organizers.
source: Overall, our results support a role for PTPRK in promoting cell-cell junctions and repressing invasive behavior, probably through recruitment and dephosphorylation of several cell junction organizers.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations including junction integrity assays and spheroid invasion assays.

claim: PTPRK displays striking substrate selectivity.
source: By combining proteomics approaches with in vitro and cell-based dephosphorylation assays we find that PTPRK displays striking substrate selectivity.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental approaches showing selective dephosphorylation.

claim: There are distinct requirements for the two PTPRK intracellular phosphatase domains for substrate recognition.
source: In addition, there are distinct requirements for the two PTPRK intracellular phosphatase domains for substrate recognition.
evidence: Inferred from experiments with individual domains and chimeric proteins.

claim: PTPRK loss perturbs epithelial junction integrity and promotes invasive behaviors in spheroid cultures.
source: Indeed, PTPRK loss perturbs epithelial junction integrity and promotes invasive behaviors in spheroid cultures, consistent with its putative tumor suppressor role.
evidence: Supported by junction integrity assays and spheroid invasion experiments.

claim: The C1089S substrate trap was effective in identifying substrates.
source: These five proteins were subsequently found to be hyperphosphorylated in PTPRK KO cells, suggesting that the C1089S mutant was effective in identifying substrates.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between trapped proteins and hyperphosphorylated proteins in KO cells.

claim: The traps alone were too restrictive in identifying substrates.
source: However, we also found hyperphosphorylation of other PTPRK-binding partners in KO cells, indicating the traps alone were too restrictive in identifying substrates.
evidence: Inferred from finding hyperphosphorylated proteins that were not trapped.

claim: The PTPRK pseudophosphatase D2 domain was sufficient for substrate recognition.
source: Indeed, the PTPRK pseudophosphatase D2 domain was sufficient for substrate recognition, which may have masked the effect of the substrate traps, particularly as we have shown that D2 domain binding to most proteins is independent of tyrosine phosphorylation.
evidence: Inferred from D2 domain pull-down experiments and phosphorylation-independent binding.

claim: Most of the candidate PTPRK substrates identified have orthologs in Drosophila, yet the R2B receptor family first appears in chordates.
source: Strikingly, most of the candidate PTPRK substrates identified here have orthologs in Drosophila, yet the R2B receptor family first appears in chordates (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on receptor evolution.

claim: PTPRK regulates pre-established functional protein complexes rather than co-evolving with its substrates.
source: This suggests that rather than co-evolving with its substrates, PTPRK regulates pre-established functional protein complexes.
evidence: Inferred from evolutionary analysis of substrates and receptor family.

claim: PTPRK would have introduced new regulation, and perhaps function, to existing signaling networks for chordate and vertebrate-specific organization.
source: In this way, PTPRK would have introduced new regulation, and perhaps function, to existing signaling networks for chordate and vertebrate-specific organization.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on evolutionary analysis.

claim: There are genetic links between orthologs for RAPGEF6, PARD3 and Afadin in the regulation of Drosophila AJ formation.
source: Indeed, there are genetic links between orthologs for RAPGEF6, PARD3 and Afadin in the regulation of Drosophila AJ formation (Bonello et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: PARD3 and p120Cat Drosophila orthologs have been linked to the control of E-Cadherin internalization and recycling.
source: Furthermore, PARD3 and p120Cat Drosophila orthologs have been linked to the control of E-Cadherin internalization and recycling (Bulgakova and Brown, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Several PTPRK substrates belong to the δ-catenin family, which undergoes significant expansion from one gene in Drosophila to seven in vertebrates.
source: Several PTPRK substrates belong to the δ-catenin family, which undergoes significant expansion from one gene in Drosophila to seven in vertebrates (Carnahan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on δ-catenin family evolution.

claim: PKP3 has been proposed to promote the stability of desmosomes upon overexpression.
source: PKP3 has been proposed to promote the stability of desmosomes upon overexpression (Gurjar et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: p120Cat controls epithelial cell lateral domain expansion and shape maturation by balancing junctional contractility and maturation through regulation of E-Cadherin and RhoA.
source: This is reminiscent of the proposed role of p120Cat in controlling epithelial cell lateral domain expansion and shape maturation by balancing junctional contractility and maturation through regulation of E-Cadherin and RhoA (Yu et al., 2016), which reportedly depends on p120Cat tyrosine phosphorylation status (Castaño et al., 2007; Davis et al., 2003; Fukumoto et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PTPRK dephosphorylates p120Cat in cells.
source: Indeed, we show that PTPRK dephosphorylates p120Cat in cells, and that PTPRK phosphatase activity is necessary to rescue junctional deficits.
evidence: Supported by rescue experiments showing phosphatase activity-dependent rescue.

claim: Afadin appears to be a unique PTPRK substrate; it was not dephosphorylated by the very closely related PTPRM.
source: Afadin appears to be a unique PTPRK substrate; it was not dephosphorylated by the very closely related PTPRM and it had the highest fold increase in tyrosine phosphorylation in PTPRK KO cells.
evidence: Supported by dephosphorylation assays and phosphoproteomics data.

claim: The specificity of Afadin dephosphorylation is determined in large part by the PTPRK D2 pseudophosphatase domain.
source: Strikingly, this specificity is determined in large part by the PTPRK D2 pseudophosphatase domain, which was sufficient to recruit Afadin for dephosphorylation by the PTPRM D1 domain.
evidence: Supported by experiments with chimeric proteins.

claim: There is little evidence for a PTPRK substrate consensus sequence other than a bias against basic residues immediately adjacent to the phosphotyrosine site.
source: In line with this, we found little evidence for a PTPRK substrate consensus sequence other than a bias against basic residues immediately adjacent to the phosphotyrosine site, similar to previous reports for other PTPs (Barr et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and citation to previous study.

claim: The Janus kinases have a similar tandem arrangement where a pseudokinase domain regulates kinase activity.
source: The Janus kinases have a similar tandem arrangement where a pseudokinase domain regulates kinase activity (Babon et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Regulation of the PTP D1 by D2 domains has been suggested for several RPTPs.
source: Indeed, regulation of the PTP D1 by D2 domains has been suggested for several RPTPs (Toledano-Katchalski et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: A three-fold reduction in PTPRK ICD enzyme activity was observed compared to the D1 domain alone.
source: We do observe a three-fold reduction in PTPRK ICD enzyme activity compared to the D1 domain alone.
evidence: Supported by pNPP assay data.

claim: When free D2 domain was added to free D1 domain, no impact on activity was observed.
source: However, when free D2 domain was added to free D1 domain, we saw no impact on activity.
evidence: Supported by pNPP assay data.

claim: A key role for the pseudophosphatase domain in substrate recognition was found, similar to findings for CD45/PTPRC.
source: Instead, we find a key role for the pseudophosphatase domain in substrate recognition, similar to findings for CD45/PTPRC (Nam et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to previous study.

claim: The PTPRK D2 domain could not easily be reactivated by mutation, unlike LAR.
source: We further show that unlike LAR (Nam et al., 1999), the PTPRK D2 domain could not easily be reactivated by mutation.
evidence: Supported by mutagenesis experiments and citation to previous study.

claim: A role for the D2 domain in phosphotyrosine recognition was ruled out using dephosphorylated lysates, vanadate competition and a PTPRK homology model.
source: Additionally, we rule out a role for the D2 domain in phosphotyrosine recognition using dephosphorylated lysates, vanadate competition and a PTPRK homology model.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental approaches and structural modeling.

claim: Wildtype PTPs can interact with substrates, which are presumably in a dephosphorylated state.
source: Several previous reports have shown that wildtype PTPs can interact with substrates, which are presumably in a dephosphorylated state (Chen et al., 2006; Lee and Bennett, 2013; Timms et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PTPRK might serve as a scaffold for dephosphorylated proteins either by recruiting non-phosphorylated proteins, or by dephosphorylating already phosphorylated proteins upon recruitment.
source: Thus, PTPRK might serve as a scaffold for dephosphorylated proteins either by recruiting non-phosphorylated proteins, or by dephosphorylating already phosphorylated proteins upon recruitment.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on experimental observations.

claim: The combination of recognition and dephosphorylation is likely important for full PTPRK function.
source: It is likely that the combination of recognition and dephosphorylation is important for full PTPRK function.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on experimental observations.

claim: PTPRK and PTPRM both dephosphorylated PARD3, p120Cat, PKP3 and PKP4 in lysates.
source: PTPRK and PTPRM both dephosphorylated PARD3, p120Cat, PKP3 and PKP4 in lysates.
evidence: Supported by in-lysate dephosphorylation assays.

claim: Hyperphosphorylation of sites on PARD3, p120Cat, PKP3 and PKP4 were found in PTPRK KO cells, indicating that PTPRM cannot fully compensate for PTPRK loss.
source: Despite this, hyperphosphorylation of sites on each of these proteins were found in PTPRK KO cells, indicating that PTPRM cannot fully compensate for PTPRK loss.
evidence: Supported by phosphoproteomics data from PTPRK KO cells.

claim: The inability of PTPRM to compensate for PTPRK loss could be due to lower PTPRM expression levels in MCF10A cells, possible differences in site selectivity or its intrinsically lower catalytic activity.
source: This could be due to lower PTPRM expression levels in MCF10A cells, possible differences in site selectivity or its intrinsically lower catalytic activity (this study and Barr et al., 2009).
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on experimental observations and citation to previous study.

claim: Vertebrate genomes all encode at least 4 R2B family members, with distinct expression profiles.
source: Vertebrate genomes all encode at least 4 R2B family members, with distinct expression profiles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by expression data and established knowledge.

claim: The R2B receptors display divergent expression patterns in the adult mouse cerebellum by in situ hybridization.
source: For example, by in situ hybridization the receptors display divergent expression patterns in the adult mouse cerebellum (Besco et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Receptor expression patterns will determine subtly distinct responses to cell contact.
source: Assuming they are regulated similarly by cell-cell contact, our results indicate that receptor expression patterns will determine subtly distinct responses to cell contact.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations about receptor specificity and expression patterns.

claim: p120Cat-Y228 is phosphorylated in response to EGFR.
source: Several phosphosites that are regulated by PTPRK have been characterized previously. p120Cat-Y228 is phosphorylated in response to EGFR and a construct with N terminal phosphorylation-deficient mutations (including Y228F) is capable of rescuing adhesion phenotypes caused by p120cat deletion (Mariner et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: A phosphomimetic p120Cat -Y228E mutant increased recruitment of RhoA.
source: In contrast, a phosphomimetic p120Cat -Y228E mutant increased recruitment of RhoA (Castaño et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Afadin Y1237 phosphorylation has been shown to mediate recruitment of SHP2, implicating it in Ras-Mitogen activated protein kinase signaling.
source: Afadin Y1237 phosphorylation, the rat equivalent of Human Afadin Y1230, has been shown to mediate recruitment of SHP2, implicating it in Ras-Mitogen activated protein kinase signaling (Nakata et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: PTPRK-mediated dephosphorylation of Afadin Y1230 supports the role of PTPRK in tumor suppression.
source: This supports the role of PTPRK-mediated dephosphorylation of this site in tumor suppression.
evidence: Inferred from previous findings about Afadin phosphorylation and PTPRK function.

claim: PTPRK is the only R2B family member implicated by transposon-based mouse forward genetics in the progression of several cancers.
source: PTPRK is the only R2B family member implicated by transposon-based mouse forward genetics in the progression of several cancers (March et al., 2011; Starr et al., 2009) and has been proposed to function as a tumor suppressor.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Specific gene fusions result in PTPRK promoter driving the expression of oncogenic RSPO3 in a subset of colorectal cancers.
source: Moreover, specific gene fusions result in its promoter driving the expression of oncogenic RSPO3 in a subset of colorectal cancers (Seshagiri et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: PTPRK is the predominant R2B receptor expressed in the mouse intestinal epithelium.
source: This is consistent with PTPRK being the predominant R2B receptor expressed in the mouse intestinal epithelium (Haber et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Findings of abrogated junction organization, spheroid overgrowth and invasive behavior in PTPRK-deficient cells support its role as a tumor suppressor.
source: Our findings of abrogated junction organization, spheroid overgrowth and invasive behavior in PTPRK-deficient cells support its role as a tumor suppressor.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Several of the PTPRK substrates identified have been linked to cancer, including PARD3 loss-of-function in invasion, and oncogenic and tumor suppressive roles for p120Cat.
source: Several of the PTPRK substrates identified here have been linked to cancer, including PARD3 loss-of-function in invasion (de la Rosa et al., 2017), and oncogenic and tumor suppressive roles for p120Cat (Schackmann et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Combined dysregulation of PTPRK substrates could contribute to pathological phenotypes in a PTPRK mutant setting.
source: Thus, their combined dysregulation could contribute to pathological phenotypes in a PTPRK mutant setting.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on substrate functions.

claim: Compromised epithelial barrier integrity is linked to inflammatory bowel disease susceptibility.
source: Compromised epithelial barrier integrity is also linked to inflammatory bowel disease susceptibility; therefore, PTPRK SNPs linked to celiac disease should be investigated (Trynka et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and citation to previous study.

claim: PTPRK functions to suppress epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT), indicating a negative feedback role that could lead to pathological effects if perturbed.
source: PTPRK is a TGFβ target gene (Wang et al., 2005), and our data suggest it functions to suppress epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT), indicating a negative feedback role that could lead to pathological effects if perturbed (Brabletz et al., 2018).
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and citations to previous studies.

claim: PTPRK does not dephosphorylate EGFR in our assays, consistent with previous peptide assays.
source: Although PTPRK does not dephosphorylate EGFR in our assays, consistent with previous peptide assays (Barr et al., 2009), we did observe an interaction by BioID.
evidence: Supported by dephosphorylation assays, BioID data, and citation to previous study.

claim: EGFR family interactions with R2B receptors have been reported.
source: Indeed, EGFR family interactions with R2B receptors have been reported (Yao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Growth factor stimulation leads to PTPRK tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: Growth factor stimulation leads to PTPRK tyrosine phosphorylation (Batth et al., 2018; Reddy et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It has been suggested that RTK-induced PTP inhibition by oxidation impacts cellular signaling.
source: and it has been suggested that RTK-induced PTP inhibition by oxidation impacts cellular signaling (Reynolds et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: PTPs are well-placed to fine-tune and tailor responses to particular cellular contexts.
source: PTPs are well-placed to fine-tune and tailor responses to particular cellular contexts.
evidence: General statement based on established knowledge of PTP function.

claim: Several PTPRK substrates are phosphorylated in a Src-dependent manner.
source: Several PTPRK substrates are phosphorylated in a Src-dependent manner (Reddy et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: PTPRK might provide feedback in the context of cell contact by dephosphorylating its substrates to promote junctional integrity.
source: PTPRK might therefore provide feedback in the context of cell contact by dephosphorylating its substrates to promote junctional integrity.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on experimental observations.

claim: Overexpression of v-Src in epithelial cells leads to junction disassembly and EMT.
source: Indeed, overexpression of v-Src in epithelial cells leads to junction disassembly and EMT (Woodcock et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: PTPs could act as interpreters of the cellular context.
source: Thus, such PTPs could act as interpreters of the cellular context.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on PTP function.

claim: An analogous role for the contact-sensing RTK EphA2 was recently reported.
source: Interestingly, an analogous role for the contact-sensing RTK EphA2 was recently reported (Stallaert et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Defining the substrate repertoire of human PTPRK reveals mechanistic insight into its putative tumor suppressor role through its control of cell-cell junctions and suppression of EMT.
source: In summary, by defining the substrate repertoire of human PTPRK, we reveal mechanistic insight into its putative tumor suppressor role through its control of cell-cell junctions and suppression of EMT.
evidence: Summary statement inferred from all experimental observations.

claim: The study raises new questions about the phosphoregulation of junctional proteins and implicates PTPRK as a direct sensor and mediator of cell adhesion.
source: Our study raises new questions about the phosphoregulation of junctional proteins and implicates PTPRK as a direct sensor and mediator of cell adhesion.
evidence: Summary statement based on experimental findings.

claim: The PTPRK D2 domain is critical for substrate recognition, yet binds proteins independently of phosphorylation status.
source: We show that the PTPRK D2 domain is critical for substrate recognition, yet binds proteins independently of phosphorylation status.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental observations.

claim: It is unknown whether the R2B receptor extracellular regions affect phosphatase activity or substrate recruitment.
source: In addition, it is unknown whether the R2B receptor extracellular regions, which were previously described as spacer clamps (Aricescu et al., 2007), affect phosphatase activity or substrate recruitment.
evidence: Statement about knowledge gap with citation to previous study.

claim: PTPRK, like other PTPs, does not recognize a peptide consensus sequence, unlike certain serine/threonine phosphatases.
source: Finally, we show that PTPRK, like other PTPs (Li et al., 2013), does not recognize a peptide consensus sequence, unlike certain serine/threonine phosphatases (Shi, 2009), highlighting the need for the approach we have taken.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and citations to previous studies.

claim: The study provides a framework for systematically identifying RPTP substrates.
source: Thus, we provide a framework for systematically identifying RPTP substrates, which in turn will advance our knowledge of these poorly characterized, yet important enzymes.
evidence: Summary statement about methodological contribution.
